nodes.title: Fluid Statics & Hydrostatic Pressure
points: A fluid is a substance that can flow and cannot withstand shear stress under static conditions.
Hydrostatic pressure P = F/A acts normal to the surface in contact. SI unit: N/m² (Pa). Dimensions: [M¹L⁻¹T⁻²].
Pressure at depth h in an open fluid: P = P₀ + hρg, where P₀ is atmospheric pressure and ρ is fluid density.
Gauge pressure = P − P₀ = hρg (excess pressure over atmospheric pressure).
Hydrostatic Paradox: Liquid pressure depends only on depth h, density ρ, and g; it is independent of the shape of the vessel.
Atmospheric pressure at sea level: 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ N/m² (Pa) = 76 cm of Hg.

nodes.title: Pascal's Law & Hydraulic Machines
points: Pascal's Law: Pressure applied to an enclosed incompressible fluid is transmitted undiminished to every portion of the fluid and container walls.
Hydraulic lift operates on Pascal's law: P₁ = P₂ ⟹ F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
Mechanical advantage = F₂/F₁ = A₂/A₁ > 1 when A₂ > A₁ (force multiplier).
Work done is conserved in an ideal machine: W₁ = W₂ ⟹ F₁ × d₁ = F₂ × d₂ (greater force, smaller displacement).
Hydraulic brakes in automobiles also use Pascal's law for uniform braking force on all wheels.

nodes.title: Surface Tension & Surface Energy
points: Cohesive force: attraction between molecules of the same substance. Adhesive force: attraction between molecules of different substances.
Sphere of influence: sphere around a molecule having radius equal to molecular range (~10⁻⁹ m).
Surface tension T is the tangential force per unit length acting perpendicular to an imaginary line drawn on the liquid surface.
SI unit of T is N/m or J/m². Dimensions: [M¹L⁰T⁻²].
Surface energy is the potential energy stored in the surface layer due to work done against inward cohesive pull.
Work done in increasing surface area: W = T × ΔA.

nodes.title: Angle of Contact & Meniscus Shapes
points: Angle of contact θ is the angle between the tangent to liquid surface and the solid surface inside the liquid.
For pure water and clean glass, θ = 0° (completely wetting, concave meniscus, adhesive > cohesive/√2).
For normal water and glass, θ is acute (θ < 90°), liquid wets the solid.
For mercury and glass, θ is obtuse (θ ≈ 140°), liquid does not wet solid, convex meniscus (cohesive > adhesive).
For completely non-wetting liquid on solid, θ = 180°.
Addition of highly soluble solute (like NaCl) increases T; sparingly soluble solute (detergent/soap) decreases T; insoluble impurities decrease T.
Surface tension decreases with increase in temperature and becomes zero at critical temperature.

nodes.title: Excess Pressure (Laplace's Law)
points: Curved liquid surface has excess pressure on the concave side compared to the convex side.
For a liquid drop (1 free surface): ΔP = P_in − P_out = 2T/R.
For a soap bubble in air (2 free surfaces): ΔP = P_in − P_out = 4T/R.
For an air bubble inside a liquid (1 free surface): ΔP = 2T/R.
Smaller drops have larger internal excess pressure (ΔP ∝ 1/R). Hence, air flows from smaller bubble to larger bubble when connected.

nodes.title: Capillarity & Capillary Ascent
points: Capillarity: The phenomenon of rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow tube (capillary) dipped in it.
Liquid rises if θ < 90° (water in glass); liquid falls if θ > 90° (mercury in glass).
Height of liquid column h = (2T cosθ)/(rρg), where r is tube radius, ρ is liquid density.
Jurin's Law: h × r = constant (liquid rises higher in a narrower tube).
If capillary tube is of insufficient length l < h, liquid rises to the top, adjusts radius of curvature R' such that h·R = l·R', but does not overflow.
Examples: sap rising in trees, ink absorption by blotting paper, oil rising in lamp wicks.

nodes.title: Fluid Dynamics & Bernoulli's Principle
points: Equation of continuity (conservation of mass): A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ = constant (volume flow rate dV/dt). Where tube narrows, flow speed increases.
Reynolds number Rₑ = ρvd/η: Rₑ < 1000 (streamline), Rₑ > 2000 (turbulent), 1000–2000 (unsteady).
Bernoulli's Theorem expresses conservation of energy for an ideal fluid: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant.
Torricelli's Law of Efflux: speed of efflux through an orifice at depth h is v = √(2gh).
Venturimeter measures flow rate of fluid through a pipe: v₁ = √[2gh / ((A₁/A₂)² − 1)].
Aerodynamic lift on an aeroplane wing: faster airflow above causes lower pressure, generating upward lift.

nodes.title: Viscosity, Stokes' Law & Terminal Velocity
points: Viscosity is internal fluid friction opposing relative motion between adjacent layers.
Newton's law of viscosity: Viscous drag F = −ηA(dv/dx). SI unit of η: Pa·s (poiseuille). 1 Pa·s = 10 poise. Dimensions: [M¹L⁻¹T⁻¹].
Stokes' Law: Viscous force on a sphere of radius r moving at speed v is F_v = 6πηrv.
Terminal velocity v_t is the constant maximum velocity achieved when net downward gravity equals upward viscous drag plus buoyancy.
Terminal velocity formula: v_t = [2r²(ρ − σ)g] / (9η), where ρ = sphere density, σ = medium density. Notice v_t ∝ r².

nodes.title: Must-Know Board Derivations & SI Units
points: Board Favourite #1: Derive Laplace's law for spherical liquid drop (ΔP = 2T/R) and soap bubble (ΔP = 4T/R).
Board Favourite #2: Derive expression for capillary ascent h = (2T cosθ)/(rρg) using pressure difference or balance of forces.
Board Favourite #3: Derive terminal velocity of a spherical body falling through a viscous medium using Stokes' law.
Essential SI Units: Surface Tension = N/m (J/m²); Viscosity = Pa·s (N·s/m²); Pressure = N/m² (Pa).
Dimensions to Memorise: Surface Tension = [M¹L⁰T⁻²]; Viscosity η = [M¹L⁻¹T⁻¹]; Pressure = [M¹L⁻¹T⁻²].

nodes.title: MHT-CET Shortcuts, Droplet Traps & Exam Hacks
points: Droplet Splitting: When 1 big drop (radius R) splits into n identical small droplets (radius r): r = R / n^(1/3).
Work Done in Splitting: W = 4πR²T(n^(1/3) − 1). Since surface area increases, heat is absorbed and temperature drops.
Droplets Merging: When n identical droplets coalesce into 1 big drop, surface area decreases, energy is released: ΔU = 4πR²T(n^(1/3) − 1), temperature rises.
Terminal Velocity Ratio: v₁/v₂ = (r₁/r₂)² for spheres of the same material falling through the same fluid.
Trap: Soap bubble has 2 free surfaces (multiply area change by 2, ΔP = 4T/R). Liquid drop or air bubble in liquid has only 1 free surface (ΔP = 2T/R).
Insufficient Capillary Length: Water does NOT spill out; the meniscus flattens to a larger radius R' such that h·R = l·R'.
